slides.title: Japanese ascetics spent years trying to become mummies.
A buddha in this very body
slides.body: That's what sokushinbutsu means: preserved bodies of ascetics, seated in robes and venerated in temples. About 17 or 18 survive in Japan.

slides.title: Years on the mountain
slides.body: Most are linked to sacred Mount Yudono. For years they kept 'tree-eating,' a diet with no cereals, and seclusions such as a thousand-day retreat.

slides.title: An offering for others
slides.body: Temples present these lives as prayers against famine and epidemics, and as a vow to remain in the world until the future buddha Maitreya comes.

slides.title: The legend you've heard
slides.body: Popular accounts say the ascetic was sealed underground with a bamboo breathing tube and a bell, then dug up three years and three months later.

slides.title: What science found
slides.body: Evidence for that is thin. A survey begun in 1959 found that at least some bodies were dried or treated by others after death, one by smoking.

caption: The legend: sealed underground with a bell. The science: messier. One of them still gets his robes changed every 12 years. Had you heard of these?
